entries.non_ste_example:
1. Read the DATABASE_URL from the environment file.
2. Use the DB_CONNECTION_STRING to connect to the database.
3. The POSTGRES_URL must include the host, port, and database name.
entries.ste_example:
1. Read the DATABASE_URL from the environment file.
2. Use the DATABASE_URL to connect to the database.
3. The DATABASE_URL must include the host, port, and database name.
entries.explanation: DATABASE_URL / DB_CONNECTION_STRING / POSTGRES_URL → DATABASE_URL (consistent technical noun per P11). Three different names refer to the same environment variable. The reader cannot tell if they are the same or different variables. Use the approved name DATABASE_URL in all three sentences.

entries.non_ste_example:
1. Call the calculateTotal function with the order items.
2. The computeSum method adds all line items.
3. Return the result from the getGrandTotal function.
entries.ste_example:
1. Call the calculateTotal function with the order items.
2. The calculateTotal function adds all line items.
3. Return the result from the calculateTotal function.
entries.explanation: calculateTotal / computeSum / getGrandTotal → calculateTotal (consistent technical noun per P11). Three different function names refer to the same operation in the codebase. The STE version uses the single approved name calculateTotal consistently, the same way the spec example uses actuator.

entries.non_ste_example:
1. Add the connection settings to the [database] section.
2. The [db_settings] block must contain the host and port.
3. Restart the service after you change the [postgresql] section.
entries.ste_example:
1. Add the connection settings to the [database] section.
2. The [database] section must contain the host and port.
3. Restart the service after you change the [database] section.
entries.explanation: [database] / [db_settings] / [postgresql] → [database] (consistent technical noun per P11). Three different section names in a configuration file refer to the same configuration block. The STE version uses [database] in all three steps.

entries.non_ste_example:
1. Build the web_app container with the updated Dockerfile.
2. Push the frontend_container to the container registry.
3. Restart the nginx_server after the deployment completes.
entries.ste_example:
1. Build the web_app container with the updated Dockerfile.
2. Push the web_app container to the container registry.
3. Restart the web_app container after the deployment completes.
entries.explanation: web_app / frontend_container / nginx_server → web_app (consistent technical noun per P11). Three different container names refer to the same deployed service. The STE version uses the approved name web_app in all three sentences.

entries.non_ste_example:
1. Use the --output-dir flag to set the build destination.
2. The --destination argument accepts a relative or an absolute path.
3. The tool writes all generated files to the --target-folder.
entries.ste_example:
1. Use the --output-dir flag to set the build destination.
2. The --output-dir flag accepts a relative or an absolute path.
3. The tool writes all generated files to the --output-dir directory.
entries.explanation: --output-dir / --destination / --target-folder → --output-dir (consistent technical noun per P11). Three different CLI flag names refer to the same option. The STE version uses the approved flag --output-dir in all three sentences.
